summary: Describes a framework for defining encryption and checksum mechanisms for Kerberos 5. It creates an abstraction layer between the protocol and the actual algorithms, and defines several mechanisms, some adapted from RFC 1510.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3961 defines what an encryption or checksum mechanism must specify to work with Kerberos 5. It also explains how mechanisms can derive separate keys for different uses.

subtitle: A framework for defining the encryption and checksum mechanisms used by Kerberos 5.

tldr.problem: Kerberos needs encryption and integrity checks, but its protocol should not depend on one particular algorithm. RFC 1510 did not fully specify how to define interoperable mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3961 defines profiles that say which operations and properties encryption and checksum mechanisms must provide. It also defines key derivation and several DES and Triple-DES mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a framework and mechanisms, but does not say which ones implementations must support. It warns that DES is no longer strong and has been updated by RFC 8429.

today: RFC 3961 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8429. Its security considerations state that DES is no longer considered a strong encryption mechanism.

sections.title: Why Kerberos Needs a Cryptographic Framework
sections.content:
Kerberos encrypts messages to help prove the identities of parties in an exchange. The protocol does not require one particular encryption algorithm, but each mechanism must provide a defined set of operations.

RFC 3961 sets out the profiles for encryption and checksums and describes mechanisms used with Kerberos. It revises some mechanisms from RFC 1510 and adds others. This document does not identify which mechanisms are required for implementation; other specifications make that choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos can use different encryption and checksum algorithms if each one provides the operations the protocol needs. This RFC defines a common checklist for those mechanisms.

sections.title: Keys and Key Usage Numbers
sections.content:
Encryption must provide confidentiality, integrity and non-malleability. A checksum mechanism must let a receiver check message integrity. The RFC recommends adding a random confounder before the plaintext so observers cannot tell when two ciphertexts contain the same plaintext.

Kerberos uses a key usage number to distinguish the purposes for which a key is used. A mechanism combines a base key with that usage number to derive a specific key for an operation. Key usage numbers are unsigned 32-bit integers, and zero is not allowed. Each encryption or checksum algorithm also has a type number for identification in Kerberos messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A key usage number identifies the purpose of a cryptographic operation. A mechanism uses it with the base key to derive a key for that particular purpose.

sections.title: Profiles for Encryption and Checksums
sections.content:
An encryption profile specifies the key format and structure, how to generate keys, how to initialize and carry cipher state, and how to encrypt and decrypt data. It also specifies string-to-key and pseudo-random functions. A decryption operation must check integrity and return an error instead of data when the check fails.

A checksum profile specifies which encryption keys it works with and defines functions to create and verify an integrity token. Its checksum cannot exceed 65,535 octets. An unkeyed checksum can be used with any encryption type, but only when the checksum itself is protected.

Specifications for new mechanisms should describe known weaknesses and provide test vectors or other validation procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile lists the details a mechanism must define, including how it handles keys, data and integrity checks. This lets implementers build compatible mechanisms without relying on hidden assumptions.

sections.title: The Simplified Profile and Derived Keys
sections.content:
The simplified profile fills in many of the full profile's operations for CBC-style ciphers using key derivation. The RFC recommends that future mechanisms use this profile or a related one. A derivation function uses the base key and a well-known constant to produce separate keys for checksums, encryption and integrity checks.

The base key is used only to derive these keys. The RFC states that compromising one derived key does not compromise the others. The simplified profile encrypts a random confounder, the plaintext and padding, then includes a keyed HMAC so the receiver can detect changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplified profile derives separate keys for encryption and integrity checks from one base key. The base key is kept for derivation rather than being used directly on message data.

sections.title: The Defined DES and Triple-DES Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC defines single-DES encryption types for backward compatibility: des-cbc-crc, des-cbc-md4 and des-cbc-md5. They use DES in CBC mode and differ in their checksum. The RFC also defines related checksum types, including unkeyed checksums that it says should be used cautiously.

The Triple-DES pair is des3-cbc-hmac-sha1-kd for encryption and hmac-sha1-des3-kd for checksums. It uses the simplified profile with key derivation. Its encryption type number is 16, its protocol key is 24 bytes and its key-generation seed is 21 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines DES mechanisms for compatibility and a Triple-DES mechanism that uses key derivation. The RFC does not require every Kerberos implementation to support these particular mechanisms.

sections.title: Algorithm Numbers and Registries
sections.content:
Kerberos identifies encryption and checksum algorithms with numeric type values. The RFC records existing and reserved values and creates separate IANA registries for encryption types and checksum types. These type numbers are signed 32-bit values; zero is invalid, negative values are for local use and standardized values are positive.

Standards-track specifications can receive values under Standards Action. Other RFC specifications can receive values after Expert Review. The RFC recommends lower numbers for IETF standards-track mechanisms and higher numbers, starting at 16777216, for other mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains separate number lists for Kerberos encryption and checksum mechanisms. A type number tells implementations which mechanism a message uses.

sections.title: Security Limits and Warnings
sections.content:
The RFC states that DES is no longer considered a strong encryption mechanism and that Triple-DES is generally preferred in its place, despite lower performance. It also says some mechanisms are weak for protecting critical data. CRC-32 is not collision-proof, and the Kerberos version described here can give the same checksum to messages that differ only in leading zero bits.

The RFC warns against using one key for multiple purposes. Reuse can expand chosen-plaintext attacks across protocol versions. A random confounder can make such attacks harder. The document does not limit the amount of data processed by a key or operation, so implementations may need message-size limits at a higher level.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC warns that DES and some checksum mechanisms have security weaknesses. It also explains why separate keys and random confounders help reduce some attacks.
